# Introduction

When a video game is created, one question lingers in the minds of its developers: "Will this game be a success?" The success of a video game can represent and influence the popularity, prestige, and resources of the companies or developers behind it. Therefore, understanding the audience and their preferences becomes a topic of paramount importance. Our report seeks to identify the factors that influence the commercial success of a video game. To do this, we will use a dataset of video games up to 2016, with diverse characteristics for each. Indicators such as sales, ratings, and developer will help us understand what types of games tend to be most successful. To address this question, we will employ exploratory analyses and graphs that will reveal the most influential factors in a video game's success. In this way, our analysis will highlight the most important factors for predicting the potential success of a new game.

# Question

- What factors influence the success of a video game?

  - Which game genres were the most commercially successful globally?

  - What regions do the top genres sell the best in?
  
  - Do video games with higher critic scores sell more copies worldwide?


# Data Preparation

Kaggle Dataset: SID_TWR. (2019, May 10). Video games sales dataset. Kaggledatasets. <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/sidtwr/videogames-sales-dataset>

Source of data: Video game charts, game sales, top sellers, game data - VGChartz. (n.d.). Www.Vgchartz.Com. Retrieved November 6, 2026, from <https://www.vgchartz.com/>

VGChartz Staff: <https://www.vgchartz.com/staff.php>

The kaggle data was originally from Gregory Smith's web scrape of VGChartz Video Game Sales, but the kaggle creator, SID_TWR, extended it with more variables from a web scrape of Metacritic. The VGChartz data come from the VGChartz team, with CEO Brett Walton; linked above is the homepage and staff page of VGChartz. The VGChartz staff pages states that, "Brett Walton created VGChartz in the summer of 2006 as a way of collating all publicly available videogame sales data into one place" (VGChartz). Kaggle creator SID_TWR states that he was motivated by Gregory Smith's web scrape to extend the data in order to be more informative. The data was last updated in 2019 but the data itself has records up to 2016. One peculiarity of the data is that there is a notable amount of missing data. As SID_TWR states, "Metacritic only covers a subset of the platforms" (SID_TWR).

Let's start by reading the data from the csv

```{r}
# Reading data from csv file using read.csv()
game_data <- read.csv("Game_Sales.csv")
```

Next, there are two games that are who's names are blank and missing important data. Most likely they only had some of the data and decided to add what they could. Since they are missing a significant amount of important data, let's remove them.

```{r}
game_data |> filter(Name == "") # Missing data in question

game_data <- game_data |> filter(Name != "") # Removing these two entries
```

Let's take a look at our cleaned data.

```{r}
# Taking a "glimpse" of the data
glimpse(game_data_tidy)
```
Thankfully, this data is tidy since each game has its own row, each variable has its own column and each value has its own cell. However, one thing we need to look out for once we start working with the data is any missing values that might affect our calculations.

One thing we need to look out for once we start working with the data is any missing values that might affect our calculations.

# Exploratory Data Analysis

## Which game genres were the most commercially successful globally?

The first question our report would like to explore is what game genres are the most commercially successful? In order to answer this question let's take a look at a plot of Total Global Sales per Genre.

```{r}
genre_sales_plot <- game_data |> # Store Data to variable to use in plotly
  group_by(Genre) |> # Group Data by Genre
  summarize(total_global_sales = sum(Global_Sales, na.rm = T)) |> # Find the Total Global Sales for each Genre
  ggplot(aes(y = reorder(Genre, total_global_sales), # Create a plot of the findings
             x = total_global_sales,
             text = paste("Total Global Sales (Million):", total_global_sales))) + # "text" displays the exact number of units sold in ggplotly
  geom_col() + # Use a column chart since we have one discrete variable and one continuous variable
  labs(title = "Total Global Sales by Genre", 
       x = "Total Global Sales (Million Units Sold)", 
       y = "Genre") # Put genre on the y-axis for readability

ggplotly(genre_sales_plot, tooltip = "text") # ggplotly makes the graph interactive, use the "text" we made before as the tooltip
```

Based on this graph, it's clear that the `Action` genre of video game sells the best, with the `Sports` and `Shooter` genres coming in second and third respectively.

## What regions do the top genres sell the best in?

Now that we know what genres sell the best, let's take a look at how they sell in each region. After all, depending on what genre a new game is, it might sell better in different regions. To do this, let's take a look at the percentage of sales by each region for the top 5 genres.

```{r}
game_data |>
  group_by(Genre) |> # Grouping data by genre to calculate sales percentage for each
  mutate(NA_Sales_Percent = (sum(NA_Sales) / sum(Global_Sales)) * 100, # Creating a column for the sales percentage for each region
         EU_Sales_Percent = (sum(EU_Sales) / sum(Global_Sales)) * 100,
         JP_Sales_Percent = (sum(JP_Sales) / sum(Global_Sales)) * 100,
         Other_Sales_Percent = (sum(Other_Sales) / sum(Global_Sales)) * 100) |> 
  filter(Genre %in% c("Action", "Sports", "Shooter", "Role-Playing")) |> # Filtering to the top 5 genres we found previously
  select(Genre, NA_Sales_Percent, EU_Sales_Percent, JP_Sales_Percent, Other_Sales_Percent) |> # Selecting only the necessary columns
  pivot_longer(cols = c(NA_Sales_Percent, EU_Sales_Percent, JP_Sales_Percent, Other_Sales_Percent), # Cleaning the data to make it tidy for our purpose
               names_to = "Region",
               values_to = "Percentage") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Genre, y = Percentage, fill = Region)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") # Using a dodged bar chart to make it easy to see which region a genre sells the best
  
```
## Do newer video games receive higher or lower user ratings?

```{r}
game_data |> 
  mutate(Game_Age = case_when(Year_of_Release <= 2000 ~ "Old", Year_of_Release > 2000 ~ "New")) |> 
  filter(!is.na(User_Score)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = User_Score, fill = Game_Age)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .5)
```

## Do video games with higher critic scores sell more copies worldwide?

```{r, warning = F, message = F}
game_data_tidy |> 
  filter(Region == "Global", !is.na(Critic_Score)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Critic_Score, y = Sales)) +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_smooth()
```



```{r}
ggplot(game_data, aes(x = Year_of_Release, y = User_Score)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Release Year vs User Score",
    x = "Year of Release",
    y = "User Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```



Possible graph

```{r}
game_data |> 
  group_by(Genre) |> 
  filter(Genre %in% c("Action", "Sports", "Shooter", "Role-Playing")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Global_Sales, y = Genre)) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_log10()
```
